headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; Claude Code’s filesystem/git access can steer gpt-engineer’s code generation and outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents read and write files in the same project context, so Claude Code can place attacker-controlled content where gpt-engineer later consumes it as prompt material or instructions. The pathway is not proven by docs, but shared filesystem/project-directory interaction makes injection plausible in default use.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or project directory, injected text can cross from agent_a to agent_b.
IF agent_b ingests repository files as prompt context without filtering, file-based instruction hijacking becomes feasible.
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent.
Add a manual review step before agent_b reads files written by agent_a.
Strip instruction-like text from shared files before handoff.
Disable automatic ingestion of newly written files where possible.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for agent-written content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches source code, git history, shell environment, and secrets, while agent_b reads and writes the project directory and sends content to a configured model backend. In a shared workspace, sensitive material from agent_a can flow into agent_b’s outputs or upstream API calls, creating a realistic leakage path.
conditions: IF agent_a writes secrets or sensitive shell state into the shared workspace, agent_b can read them.
IF agent_b forwards project contents to its model backend, shared sensitive files may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared project directory.
Use a redacted handoff folder between agents.
Rotate any credentials exposed in repo or shell state.
Restrict agent_b to a sanitized subset of files.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level secret scanning before model calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and agent_a also modifies git state while sharing state via filesystem and git. That creates a direct conflict surface for concurrent edits, commits, and file overwrites in the same repo, with potentially irreversible repository damage or lost work.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory concurrently, file clobbering can occur.
IF agent_a commits or rewrites git state while agent_b edits the same repo, history conflicts can corrupt work.
mitigations: Serialize access to the repository.
Assign each agent a separate branch.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git worktrees for isolation.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared filesystem and git operations.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_b is a code generator that can treat agent_a’s repository edits as input, and agent_a can produce shell/git changes that look authoritative. Without an explicit verification step, mistakes or hallucinations from agent_a can cascade into agent_b-generated code or actions, causing multiple downstream work products to be wrong.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a’s written files as authoritative context, errors can propagate into generated code.
IF agent_a’s outputs are not reviewed before agent_b acts on them, downstream mistakes multiply.
mitigations: Require human review of agent_a outputs before handoff.
Ask agent_b to restate assumptions before generating code.
Compare generated changes against the original task.
Limit agent_a to drafting only, not final edits.
requires-engineering: add automated verification between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not show a residency or certification mismatch by themselves. The main compliance concern is that agent_a handles git credentials and shell environment while agent_b handles project files, but no specific regulated-data flow or jurisdiction conflict is documented here.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared project directory, compliance review is required.
IF either agent is used on data subject to stricter residency or retention rules, the current profiles do not document those controls.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in the workspace.
Document retention and deletion expectations before use.
Separate credentials from project files.
Review vendor terms for the specific deployment.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for regulated datasets.
